50805: Ask what the picture meant in its world and what it says about God’s character or purpose. Do not turn poetic or visionary images into literal timetables or physics.
50807: The Bible honestly records sin and failure, often without comment. Look at the consequences in the story and at the wider canon before drawing a lesson.
50809: The text records a real stage in God’s dealings with his people. Jesus is the fullness of that revelation; follow his teaching and character, and read the earlier text as pointing toward him. Traditions explain this differently (fulfilment, accommodation, progressive revelation), but all let Christ have the final word.
50810: Find the principle, translate the practice
50811: Ask what the command aimed at in that setting (order, love, witness, holiness), then ask how that same aim is best served in your setting.
50812: Receive it and obey from union

50814: Hold it humbly and ask others
50815: Some texts remain hard. Read what Christians of several traditions have said, talk with your community, and hold your conclusion with humility. It is fine to say “I do not know yet”.

50851: Read “in the same Spirit in which it was written”, within the Church
50853: Scripture, read with tradition, reason and experience
50854: Scripture is primary; the other three help us understand it
50855: Fee and Stuart, *How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth*
50856: Exegesis (what it meant then), then hermeneutics (what it means now), genre by genre
50857: Genre-specific rules for each kind of writing
50858: Richard Hays, *The Moral Vision of the New Testament*
50859: Descriptive, synthetic (whole canon), hermeneutical (bridge to now), pragmatic (live it)
50860: Three focal images: community, cross, new creation
50862: Word, Spirit and community in conversation
50863: Expectation that God speaks and acts today
50865: Pray, presuppositions, text, genre, context, canon, Christ, community, Spirit, love test, apply
50866: Jesus as the lens; identity in Christ before action
50868: Mainstream evangelical scholarship (Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart; Grant Osborne, *The Hermeneutical Spiral*, 1991)
50869: Find the meaning the human author intended for the first audience, using grammar, history and genre. Then apply that meaning carefully to today.
50870: Disciplined and testable. Guards against reading our ideas into the text. Respects the human authors.
50871: Can stop at ‘what it meant’ and never reach Christ or the Spirit. The New Testament writers themselves read the Old Testament in ways that go beyond the human author’s intent.
50872: Kevin Vanhoozer; Daniel Treier; Stephen Fowl; drawing on the church fathers
50873: Read the Bible as Christian Scripture, within the creeds and the church’s worship, aiming to know God, not only past history.
50874: Recovers the church’s long tradition of reading. Keeps Christ and the Trinity at the centre.
50875: Some historians worry it lets doctrine overrule the text. Its methods can be less clearly defined.
50877: Peter Enns; Greg Boyd; Brad Jersak; Brian Zahnd; Tommy Miller; in other forms Graeme Goldsworthy and Tim Keller
50878: Christ is the goal (Greek *telos*) and lens of all Scripture. Every text is read in its context and then in light of Jesus, the exact image of the Father.
50879: Follows the pattern of Luke 24:27 and John 5:39. Gives a clear centre for weighing hard texts.
50880: Different holders mean different things by it: for Goldsworthy and Keller it confirms the whole Old Testament, while for Boyd and Jersak it reinterprets parts of it. Critics ask who defines ‘Christlike’.
50881: Catholic and Orthodox: Scripture within Tradition
50882: *Dei Verbum* (1965); Pontifical Biblical Commission, *The Interpretation of the Bible in the Church* (1993); Orthodox writers such as Georges Florovsky
50883: The Bible is the Church’s book. It is read with the Fathers, the liturgy and the teaching Church, which guards against private misinterpretation.
50884: Gives a strong safeguard against individualism and a deep well of past readings.
50885: Protestants ask how Scripture can correct the Church if the Church is its final interpreter.
50887: Kenneth Archer (*A Pentecostal Hermeneutic*, 2004); Craig Keener (*Spirit Hermeneutics*, 2016)
50888: The Spirit who inspired Scripture still speaks through it. Reading is a conversation between Word, Spirit and community, expecting God to act as he did in the text.
50889: Recovers expectancy and the experience of God in reading. Keener insists it must include careful historical study.
50890: Without discipline, ‘the Spirit told me’ can override the text. Its best practitioners agree and tie the Spirit to Christ and Scripture.
50891: “A good method guarantees the right answer.”
50892: Some readers hope that if they follow the right steps, every difficult text will resolve and every disagreement end.
50893: Even the apostles had to work things out together (Acts 15), and Peter found some of Paul hard (2 Pet 3:16). A method makes us more honest and more humble; it does not remove all mystery (1 Cor 13:12).
50894: Scholars of every tradition agree that methods are tools, not guarantees. Evangelicals stress that Scripture is clear on what is necessary for salvation; Catholics and Orthodox add the Church’s guidance; Pentecostals add the Spirit. None claims a method removes the need for faith and humility.
50895: Expecting a formula can make us proud when we think we have it right, and despairing when we cannot resolve a text. The goal is faithfulness, not control.
50896: “The Spirit step means I can skip the study steps.”
50897: Some believers think that if the Spirit speaks to them, history, language and context do not matter.
50898: The same Spirit inspired the text in its original context. The Bereans received the word eagerly and also searched the Scriptures daily (Acts 17:11). Jesus opened the Scriptures to the Emmaus disciples by explaining them “beginning at Moses and all the prophets” (Luke 24:27).
50899: Pentecostal scholars such as Craig Keener argue the Spirit works through careful study, not around it. Traditional evangelicals stress that the Spirit illumines what the text means; he does not add new meanings that contradict it.
50900: Spirit and study belong together. Separating them produces either dry scholarship or unchecked private revelation.
